extracted.intended_audience: students and readers of the history of moral philosophy; scholars interested in doctrines of utilitarianism, Hobbesian theory, and associationist accounts of moral sentiment
extracted.subtask_description: Extracts and collects historical doctrines and quoted formulations about the origin and nature of virtue, moral motivation, and moral sentiment from philosophers (Hobbes, Bentham, Hume, Adam Smith, Helvétius, Paley, Mill, etc.). Useful for understanding competing theories of self-interest, sympathy, association, and the sanctions that bind conduct.

rubrics_metrics.name: Virtue as an end (disinterested virtue)
rubrics_metrics.description: “As virtue is an end, and is desirable on its own account without fee or reward, merely for the immediate satisfaction it conveys, it is requisite that there should be some sentiment which it touches, some internal taste or feeling... which distinguishes moral good and evil, and which embraces the one and rejects the other.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Argues that for virtue to be valued for its own sake there must exist an internal moral sentiment or taste that distinguishes good and evil independently of external rewards. (Quoted as statement of the intuitionist/ moral-sense position.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Lawgivers create moral sanctions by flattering human nature
rubrics_metrics.description: “The chief thing therefore which lawgivers and other wise men... have endeavoured, has been to make the people they were to govern believe that it was more beneficial for everybody to conquer than to indulge his appetites... observing that none were either so savage as not to be charmed with praise, or so despicable as patiently to bear contempt, they justly concluded that flattery must be the most powerful argument that could be used to human creatures.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explains a sociological account: moral notions (honour, shame) are inculcated by elites who flatter and direct vanity to secure public-spirited behavior; moral rules operate via reputational and emotive sanctions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hobbesian psychological egoism (actions from self-interest)
rubrics_metrics.description: “When a man deliberates whether he shall do a thing or not do it, he does nothing else but consider whether it be better for himself to do it or not to do it.”; “Good and evil are names that signify our appetites and aversions.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Presents Hobbes’s view that all action is motivated by private advantage; moral terms track appetites/aversions and obligation is tied to pursuit of one’s own happiness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Principle of utility (Bentham)
rubrics_metrics.description: “Nature has placed mankind under the governance of two sovereign masters, pain and pleasure... The principle of utility recognises this subjection, and assumes it for the foundation of that system... By the principle of utility is meant that principle which approves or disapproves of every action whatsoever, according to the tendency which it appears to have to augment or diminish the happiness of the party whose interest is in question.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: States utilitarian standard: moral approval/disapproval depends on an action’s tendency to increase or decrease happiness (pleasure/pain), taking pain and pleasure as fundamental motivators.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pleasure and pain as sole intrinsic good and evil (Bentham)
rubrics_metrics.description: “Pleasure is in itself a good; nay, even setting aside immunity from pain, the only good; pain is in itself an evil... the only evil, or else the words good and evil have no meaning.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An uncompromising hedonistic formulation used to underpin utilitarian moral calculation: all value reduces to pleasure and pain.

rubrics_metrics.name: Moral good/evil as conformity to laws with attendant pleasure/pain (Locke/Bentham)
rubrics_metrics.description: “Good and evil are nothing but pleasure and pain... Moral good and evil then is only the conformity or disagreement of our voluntary actions to some law whereby good or evil, pleasure or pain, attending our observance or breach of the law... is that we call reward or punishment.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Links legal/legislative sanctions to moral categories: the law-maker’s imposition of rewards/punishments maps onto moral evaluations in terms of pleasure and pain.

rubrics_metrics.name: Enlightened self-love as motive of moral sacrifice (D’Alembert/Helvétius)
rubrics_metrics.description: “Je regarde l’amour éclairé de nous-mêmes comme le principe de tout sacrifice moral.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Frames self-regarding motives (‘enlightened self-love’) as the basis for apparent sacrifices: the love of self, properly enlightened, can ground actions that look altruistic.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sanctions that bind conduct: law, religion, and public opinion
rubrics_metrics.description: Bentham/Mill: rewards and penalties of the law (political sanction), the expected sanctions from the ruler of the universe (religious sanction), and the moral sanction (public opinion) are the three powers binding conduct.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identifies three social/regulative mechanisms (political, religious, popular) by which individual pursuit of pleasure is channeled toward social order; these are central to utilitarian accounts of moral motivation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pity as imaginative self-regard (Hobbes)
rubrics_metrics.description: “Pity is imagination or fiction of future calamity to ourselves, proceeding from the sense of another man’s calamity... the compassion is greater... because there then appeareth more probability that the same may happen to us.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hobbes’s analysis treats compassion/pity as a projection of our own possible suffering onto another; a partly self-regarding motive rather than pure altruism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sympathy by imaginatively entering another’s situation (Adam Smith/Hume)
rubrics_metrics.description: “When I condole with you for the loss of your son... I not only change circumstances with you, but I change persons and characters. My grief, therefore, is entirely upon your account.... A man may sympathise... though it is impossible he should conceive himself suffering her pains in his own proper person and character.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Presents the sympathetic account: moral sympathy involves imaginatively placing oneself in another’s position (not merely projecting one’s own likely suffering) and can ground genuinely other-regarding sentiments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Friendship as reciprocal exchange of interests
rubrics_metrics.description: “Ce que les hommes ont nommé amitié n’est qu’une société, qu’un ménagement réciproque d’intérêts et qu’un échange de bons offices.... Ce n’est enfin qu’un commerce où l’amour-propre se propose toujours quelque chose à gagner.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Offers a skeptical/realist account: friendship is characterized as mutually advantageous exchange rather than pure disinterested affection (La Rochefoucauld, Helvétius).

rubrics_metrics.name: Moral philosophy as the science of legislation (Helvétius)
rubrics_metrics.description: “La science de la morale n’est autre chose que la science même de la législation.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: States the doctrinal claim that moral inquiry reduces to the study of laws and legislative devices for securing public welfare—ties normative inquiry to social regulation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hobbesian school: private appetite as measure of good and evil; peace and its means as good
rubrics_metrics.description: “Good and evil are names that signify our appetites and aversions... so long as man is in this condition of mere nature (which is a condition of war), his private appetite is the measure of good and evil. And consequently all men agree in this, that peace is good, and therefore also that the ways or means of peace... are good.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explains how, from a Hobbesian starting point, social virtues (justice, equity, mercy) are instrumentally good because they secure peace, which serves private interest.

rubrics_metrics.name: Association/translation of desire: means become ends (Hutcheson, Gay, Hartley, Tucker)
rubrics_metrics.description: Doctrines of association assert that desires initially directed to an end may be transferred to the means; 'It is the nature of translation to throw desire from the end upon the means... Our habits and most of the desires that occupy human life are of this translated kind.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provides a psychological mechanism for how altruistic actions and moral habits can arise: through association, the action itself or its concomitant sentiments become pleasurable, so motives change over time from instrumentally to intrinsically valued.

rubrics_metrics.name: Associationist account of disinterested benevolence (Hartley, Mill)
rubrics_metrics.description: Hartley: associations and honour/esteem can make benevolence pleasurable and engage us to forego pleasure for others; Mill: 'the unselfish part of our nature... the idea of the pain of another is naturally painful.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Argues that even if conduct originates in self-interest, associative psychology can produce motives experienced as disinterested benevolence—thus allowing for 'pure' benevolence as a psychological fact.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conscience as varying psychological/epistemic concept
rubrics_metrics.description: Hobbes: 'conscience is the opinion of evidence.' Locke: 'our own opinion or judgment of the moral rectitude or pravity of our own actions.' Bentham: conscience a 'thing of fictitious existence' or 'love of power.' Bain: conscience is 'an imitation within ourselves of the government without us.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Collects competing definitions showing that 'conscience' is interpreted as evidential judgment, internalized social government, fictitious faculty, or a variant of self-regarding motives depending on the theorist.

rubrics_metrics.name: Virtue as instrument to happiness but capable of becoming part of happiness (Mill)
rubrics_metrics.description: “Virtue, according to the utilitarian doctrine, is not naturally and originally part of the end, but it is capable of becoming so.... What was once desired as an instrument for the attainment of happiness has come to be desired ... as part of happiness.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: States the utilitarian conciliatory move: even if virtue begins as instrumental, habit/association can integrate it into an individual's conception of happiness, making virtue both instrument and component of well-being.

rubrics_metrics.name: Motives and disposition explained by habit and association (Mill, Adam Smith)
rubrics_metrics.description: Mill: differences in what motives operate are owing to habits of association; the facility of being acted upon by motives of a particular description is 'disposition.' Adam Smith: 'The great secret of education is to direct vanity to proper objects.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explains individual variation in moral responsiveness as the product of differing associative histories and education; moral character is thus shaped by habituation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Vice as miscalculation of pleasures and pains (Bentham)
rubrics_metrics.description: “Vice may be defined to be a miscalculation of chances, a mistake in estimating the value of pleasures and pains. It is false moral arithmetic.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Frames moral failure as an error in calculating aggregate pleasure/pain; moral improvement is thus correction of estimative errors in utilitarian terms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Weighing pains and pleasures as test of right and wrong (Bentham)
rubrics_metrics.description: “Weigh pains, weigh pleasures, and as the balance stands will stand the question of right and wrong.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explicit statement of utilitarian decision procedure: moral rightness is determined by comparative balancing of pleasures and pains produced by actions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Difference between prudence and duty tied to temporal scope of consequences (Paley)
rubrics_metrics.description: Paley: difference between an act of prudence and an act of duty is that in the latter we consider what we shall gain or lose in the world to come as well as the present world.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Shows how religious sanction (consideration of afterlife consequences) can convert prudential calculations into duties; illustrates interplay of temporal horizons and moral categorization.
